# 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document tracks the Wisconsin 2023 State Freight Plan (SFP) and its in-progress 2027 update as a state planning and investment-guidance framework, not a binding regulation with private-party penalties. It exists to give a freight forwarder with Wisconsin exposure (road, rail, air, harbor, or intermodal) a single place to see: what WisDOT has committed to, what the federal statute requires of WisDOT in producing this plan, and when the next public participation windows open.

FACT: "The Wisconsin Department of Transportation (WisDOT) is updating its 2023 State Freight Plan, with an expected completion date of summer 2027. This plan will reflect updates from the previous plan and WisDOT's 2018 original State Freight Plan. It will provide a vision for WisDOT's freight program for the next eight years." *Source: Wisconsin State Freight Plan, WisDOT Plans. https://wisdotplans.gov/plan/state-freight-plan

**What the workspace should expect to decide:** whether to submit comments during the 2027 update's public comment window, and whether pursuing Freight Advisory Committee (FAC) membership is worth the two-year seat commitment ahead of that window.

*Analytical inference:* the phrase "what the federal statute requires of WisDOT" above describes an obligation running to WisDOT under federal law, not a duty the workspace itself must satisfy.

# 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The SFP is a federally required, state-authored planning document, not a rulemaking. It applies to the workspace indirectly: it does not create compliance duties for a freight forwarder, but it does set the public investment priorities that shape which Wisconsin corridors, rail lines, harbors, and airports receive federal and state funding over the plan horizon.

FACT: "The 2027 update continues to focus on the needs of state highways and local roads, freight rail, aviation, harbors, and intermodal connections." *Source: Wisconsin State Freight Plan, WisDOT Plans. https://wisdotplans.gov/plan/state-freight-plan

*Operational implication:* A workspace routing freight through Wisconsin on any of these modes should treat the SFP as the primary public signal of where infrastructure investment (and therefore future capacity, congestion relief, and maintenance quality) is headed, not as a source of obligations that applies to the workspace directly.

# 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

FACT: "Stakeholder outreach will continue into summer of 2026 with an official comment period in late 2026." *Source: Wisconsin State Freight Plan, WisDOT Plans. https://wisdotplans.gov/plan/state-freight-plan

*Operational implication:* The near-term action item is calendar, not compliance: a workspace that wants its Wisconsin freight priorities reflected in the 2027 plan needs to submit input before the late-2026 comment window closes, since WisDOT is not obligated to solicit further comment after the plan is finalized and submitted to U.S. DOT.

FACT: "If your organization is interested in hearing more about the Wisconsin State Freight Plan, please contact us at freight@dot.wi.gov ." *Source: Wisconsin State Freight Plan, WisDOT Plans. https://wisdotplans.gov/plan/state-freight-plan

# 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

*Legal Confirmation Required:* The SFP is a planning instrument WisDOT must produce to remain eligible for National Highway Freight Program (NHFP) funding under 23 U.S.C. 167 and 49 U.S.C. 70202. It obligates WisDOT to U.S. DOT, not the workspace to WisDOT. Whether any specific Wisconsin-funded infrastructure project condition ever flows down to a private freight operator (for example, through a state contract or permit tied to NHFP-funded work) is a fact-specific question outside this brief's scope and requires counsel review on the specific project.

*Analytical inference:* Because the SFP's compliance chain runs WisDOT to U.S. DOT rather than WisDOT to the workspace, the workspace's practical leverage point in this chain is participation (FAC membership, public comment), not compliance monitoring.

# 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis

FACT: "each State that receives funding for the NHFP shall develop a comprehensive freight plan that provides for the immediate and long-range planning activities and investments of the State with respect to freight" *Source: U.S. DOT, Guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees

*Per the workspace's reading:* this is the controlling federal instrument for what the SFP must contain; it is a guidance document interpreting 49 U.S.C. 70202, not itself a new statute, and it states its own contents apply "except for any requirements specified in the statutes cited in the guidance document."

FACT: "The Wisconsin Department of Transportation's (WisDOT) report Intermodal Freight in Wisconsin - 2025 Update serves as an update to the 2019 Overview of Intermodal Freight in Wisconsin" and "supports the policies found in WisDOT's 2023 State Freight Plan." *Source: WisDOT Intermodal Freight webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/inter-sub.aspx

# 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

FACT: "FAC Meetings April 21, 2026" *Source: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx

*Operational implication:* This is the next scheduled public FAC meeting feeding the 2027 SFP update; agendas and minutes from this meeting are the earliest available signal of what will change between the 2023 and 2027 plans.

FACT: "Stakeholder outreach will continue into summer of 2026 with an official comment period in late 2026." *Source: Wisconsin State Freight Plan, WisDOT Plans. https://wisdotplans.gov/plan/state-freight-plan

*Operational implication:* The workspace should calendar the late-2026 comment window now; WisDOT plans to finalize the draft 2027 plan and submit it to U.S. DOT for approval in the following cycle, after which the workspace's ability to shape plan content ends until the next four-year cycle.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* This brief's own corpus does not include the full regulatory text of Federal Register document 2026-03648 beyond the excerpts quoted in Sections 5 and 8; a workspace with a specific compliance question about how this guidance affects a Wisconsin-funded project should confirm current status directly against the Federal Register record rather than relying solely on this summary.

# 7. Threshold Questions

**Q1: Does this framework create direct regulatory obligations on private freight operators?**

*Legal Confirmation Required:* The SFP is a state planning document developed under federal authorization. Its obligations, described in Section 8, run to WisDOT, not to freight forwarders, carriers, or logistics operators. Whether any specific Wisconsin IIJA-funded freight project's own contract or permit terms create a binding obligation on a private operator is a separate, fact-specific question requiring counsel review.

**Q2: Is the workspace a defined stakeholder category under the FAC structure?**

FACT: "FAC members include representatives from sectors including industry, agriculture, logistics, warehousing, economic development and transportation." *Source: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether a specific workspace in a freight-forwarding role qualifies for FAC membership under WisDOT's current criteria, and whether participation would be voting or non-voting, requires direct confirmation with WisDOT (freight@dot.wi.gov) and review of the FAC Charter.

**Q3: Does the plan's four-year update requirement apply to the workspace directly?**

*Analytical inference:* No. The four-year update requirement in Section 8 obligates WisDOT as the plan's author under 49 U.S.C. 70202; it applies to the workspace only in the sense that it sets the cadence at which the workspace's own Wisconsin infrastructure assumptions should be refreshed.

# 8. Substantive Requirements

*Note: this is a state planning framework, not a binding regulatory instrument. "Substantive requirements" here means the plan's own stated obligations on WisDOT (the obligated agency under federal law) plus the operational implications those obligations carry for a freight forwarder as a user of the resulting infrastructure and planning process.*

**1. Comprehensive freight plan obligation (WisDOT, federal).** FACT: "each State that receives funding for the NHFP shall develop a comprehensive freight plan that provides for the immediate and long-range planning activities and investments of the State with respect to freight" *Source: U.S. DOT, Guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees

*Legal Confirmation Required:* this obligation runs from U.S. DOT to WisDOT under 49 U.S.C. 70202; it does not itself create a duty running from WisDOT, or from U.S. DOT, to a private freight forwarder.

**2. Multimodal scope requirement.** FACT: "State Freight Plans developed pursuant to 49 U.S.C. 70202 are multimodal in scope." *Source: U.S. DOT, Guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees

FACT: "The Wisconsin State Freight Plan (SFP) is the statewide multimodal freight plan, required by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA)" *Source: Wisconsin 2023 State Freight Plan (full PDF). https://wisconsindot.gov/Documents/projects/sfp/2023-plan.pdf

*Operational implication:* the SFP's own scope is statewide and covers every freight mode WisDOT administers (highway, rail, aviation, harbor, and intermodal); a workspace operating in only one mode still falls within the plan's scope for that mode.

**3. Eight-year forecast requirement.** FACT: "``State freight plan described in subsection (a) shall address an 8-year forecast period''" *Source: U.S. DOT, Guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees

*Analytical inference:* this is why WisDOT frames the 2027 update as providing "a vision for WisDOT's freight program for the next eight years" (Section 1); the eight-year forecast window is a federal minimum, not a WisDOT choice.

**4. Four-year update cycle (statutory trajectory).** FACT: "Pursuant to 49 U.S.C. 70202, as amended by IIJA, State Freight Plans are required to be updated no less frequently than every four years." *Source: U.S. DOT, Guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees

FACT: "WisDOT anticipates updating the plan on a four-year cycle, in accordance with federal requirements, including an update to the fiscally-constrained project list and supporting documentation." *Source: Wisconsin 2023 State Freight Plan (full PDF). https://wisconsindot.gov/Documents/projects/sfp/2023-plan.pdf

*Operational implication:* the workspace should treat 2023-plan-based infrastructure assumptions as current through the 2027 adoption, and refresh them on that same four-year cadence thereafter (per-year trajectory: see the accounting note below).

**5. Funding-eligibility consequence for a missed update (the plan's "penalty" mechanism).** FACT: "If a State's four-year update cycle has expired, then unless the State has developed its State Freight Plan consistent with the existing requirements, the State may not obligate NHFP funds (23 U.S.C. 167(h)(4))." *Source: U.S. DOT, Guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees

*Legal Confirmation Required:* this consequence is a funding-eligibility freeze on WisDOT, not a fine, penalty, or enforcement action against any private freight operator. No source in this brief's corpus states a compliance deadline, fine, or penalty running to a freight forwarder, carrier, or logistics intermediary under the SFP.

**6. Freight Investment Plan exemption for certain projects.** FACT: "If a State wishes to obligate NHFP funds for a project (other than those exempt from inclusion in the Freight Investment Plan), including a freight intermodal or freight rail project" *Source: U.S. DOT, Guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees

*Analytical inference:* WisDOT's Freight Investment Plan component (the fiscally-constrained project list referenced in obligation 4 above) does not need to list every NHFP-funded project; some project categories are exempt from that listing requirement by the statute itself.

**7. Guidance effective date.** FACT: "Unless otherwise stated in this Notice, this guidance is effective February 24, 2026." *Source: U.S. DOT, Guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees

*Operational implication:* this guidance was already in effect when WisDOT's FAC met on April 21, 2026 (Section 6), so the 2027 plan's drafting process is proceeding under it.

**Qualification accounting.** Per-year trajectory: CAPTURED (see metadata.requirement_trajectory: the four-year statutory cycle, 2018 original plan to 2023 update to 2027 next update, with no sub-cycle phase-in of individual provisions). Exceptions and carve-outs: CAPTURED above (obligation 6, the Freight Investment Plan exemption). Scope limits: CAPTURED above (obligation 2, the multimodal-scope statement).

Obligations surveyed: 10; workspace-adjacent: 9; extracted as FACT: 9.

# 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

FACT: "FAC members include representatives from sectors including industry, agriculture, logistics, warehousing, economic development and transportation." *Source: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx

FACT: "Each FAC member serves for a period of up to two years." *Source: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx

FACT: "Non-voting members from government offices provide guidance from federal and state programmatic and regulatory perspectives." *Source: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx

*Operational implication:* FAC membership is the only registration-shaped mechanism in this corpus, and it is voluntary; there is no mandatory registration or reporting obligation on a private freight operator under the SFP.

FACT: "Membership list (Updated March 2026)" *Source: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx

## Public Comment Submission

FACT: "Stakeholder outreach will continue into summer of 2026 with an official comment period in late 2026." *Source: Wisconsin State Freight Plan, WisDOT Plans. https://wisdotplans.gov/plan/state-freight-plan

*Operational implication:* submitting public comment during the late-2026 window is the lowest-friction way for a non-FAC-member workspace to have Wisconsin freight priorities considered before the 2027 plan is finalized.

# 11. Operational System Requirements

*Note: because this is a planning framework rather than a binding regulatory instrument, "operational system requirements" here means the monitoring and engagement infrastructure a workspace should maintain to track this plan, not a technical or reporting system the plan itself requires.*

**1. Monitoring calendar.** *Operational implication:* set a recurring check against the WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee page for meeting agendas, and against the SFP page for the fall/late-2026 draft release and comment period.

FACT: "FAC Meetings April 21, 2026" *Source: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx

**2. FAC engagement channel.** FACT: "Dave Schroeder Freight Program Officer" is the FAC contact, reachable at "(608) 267-4541". *Source: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx

*Operational implication:* a workspace considering FAC participation should contact WisDOT well before the next membership cycle, since each seat runs up to two years (Section 10).

**3. Intermodal capacity baseline.** FACT: "The Wisconsin Department of Transportation's (WisDOT) report Intermodal Freight in Wisconsin - 2025 Update serves as an update to the 2019 Overview of Intermodal Freight in Wisconsin" *Source: WisDOT Intermodal Freight webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/inter-sub.aspx

*Operational implication:* a workspace still using the 2019 intermodal report as its Wisconsin capacity baseline is working from data superseded by the 2025 update.

# 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

FACT: "If a State wishes to obligate NHFP funds for a project (other than those exempt from inclusion in the Freight Investment Plan), including a freight intermodal or freight rail project" *Source: U.S. DOT, Guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees

*Analytical inference:* this exemption is scoped to WisDOT's own Freight Investment Plan listing requirement; it has no direct edge case for a private freight operator, since the underlying obligation it exempts from is itself a WisDOT-to-U.S.-DOT reporting requirement, not a private-party duty.

# 13. Adjacent Industry Research and Alternatives

FACT: "In late 2017, WisDOT created the Intermodal Subcommittee under the umbrella of the greater Freight Advisory Committee (FAC)" *Source: WisDOT Intermodal Freight webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/inter-sub.aspx

FACT: "FAC Charter (Updated May 2017)" *Source: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage. https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx

*Analytical inference:* the Intermodal Subcommittee's working method (a standing FAC subcommittee producing periodic reports) is a template for how a workspace's own Wisconsin-specific intermodal data could reach WisDOT's planning process outside the formal comment window.

FACT: "The Mid-America Freight Coalition (MAFC) is a regional organization that cooperates in the planning, operation, preservation, and improvement of transportation infrastructure" *Source: Mid-America Freight Coalition, About page. https://midamericafreight.org/index.php/about/

FACT: "These ten state have signed a Memorandum of Understanding in October 2006, demonstrating their willingness to meet freight demand through regional cooperative efforts." *Source: Mid-America Freight Coalition, About page. https://midamericafreight.org/index.php/about/

FACT: "The Mid-America Freight Coalition was formerly known as the Mississippi Valley Freight Coalition. The name of the coalition changed on October 25, 2010." *Source: Mid-America Freight Coalition, About page. https://midamericafreight.org/index.php/about/

*Analytical inference:* Wisconsin's SFP does not operate in isolation; it sits inside this ten-state MAFC coordination layer, which is the relevant adjacent-research body for a workspace tracking multi-state Midwest corridor investment rather than Wisconsin alone.

# 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 2018: WisDOT releases its original State Freight Plan.
- 2023: Wisconsin 2023 State Freight Plan adopted.
- February 24, 2026: U.S. DOT publishes Federal Register guidance on Multimodal State Freight Plans and State Freight Advisory Committees, Federal Register document 2026-03648, effective the same date.
- April 21, 2026: WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee meeting (agenda posted) as part of the 2027 State Freight Plan update process.
- 2026: WisDOT plans to finalize the draft 2027 State Freight Plan and release it for public comment, with an official comment period planned for late 2026.
- 2027: WisDOT plans to submit the finalized 2027 State Freight Plan to U.S. DOT for approval and adoption, restarting the statutory four-year update clock.

*Source for timeline entries: Wisconsin State Freight Plan, WisDOT Plans (https://wisdotplans.gov/plan/state-freight-plan); WisDOT Freight Advisory Committee webpage (https://wisconsindot.gov/Pages/doing-bus/freight/fac.aspx); U.S. DOT Federal Register document 2026-03648 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/02/24/2026-03648/guidance-on-multimodal-state-freight-plans-and-state-freight-advisory-committees).*

# 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document provides a regulatory fact brief on the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) final rule "Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards for Heavy-Duty Vehicles Phase 3" (also referred to as "HD Phase 3" or "GHG Phase 3"), published at 89 FR 29440. It covers the rule's substantive requirements, compliance timeline, affected entities, and operational implications for workspaces engaged in freight forwarding, logistics, and cargo operations that rely on heavy-duty road transport as a primary or secondary transport mode.

**Convention notes:**
- "The workspace" refers throughout to the workspace profile's operational and commercial characteristics, never to a named company or individual.
- Model year (MY) references follow the rule's own convention.
- Items requiring legal determination are labeled *Legal Confirmation Required:* and are not resolved in this document.
- All FACT claims carry an inline verbatim citation from the captured source pool. ANALYSIS claims carry a labeled prefix (*Analytical inference:*, *Operational implication:*, or *Industry interpretation:*).
- The captured source pool for this item contains three URLs: the EPA rule summary page, the Federal Register full text of the final rule, and a third URL that on inspection is a GAO report on an unrelated Oil and Natural Gas Sector rulemaking, not this rule. That third source is excluded from grounding and from the Sources section below; see the Sources section for the full note.

# 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The EPA finalized the "Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards for Heavy-Duty Vehicles Phase 3" rule as a final rule. The Federal Register's own citation header states, verbatim: "Federal Register, Volume 89 Issue 78 (Monday, April 22, 2024)". The rule establishes progressively more stringent GHG emission standards for heavy-duty (HD) vehicles and engines.

**effective_date (required slot):** The captured Federal Register text states, verbatim: "This final rule is effective on June 21, 2024."

**primary_deadline (required slot):** The captured Federal Register SUMMARY states, verbatim: "The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is promulgating new greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions standards for model year (MY) 2032 and later heavy-duty highway vehicles that phase in starting as early MY 2027 for certain vehicle categories." The first Phase 3 compliance year is MY 2027.

**jurisdictional_scope (required slot):** The captured Federal Register text states, verbatim: "the emission standards apply to vehicles sold in the United States regardless of where such vehicles are produced." *Operational implication:* The rule covers vehicles sold into the U.S. market regardless of manufacturing origin; it does not itself extend to state-level programs such as California's Advanced Clean Trucks (ACT) program, a separate instrument discussed in the Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis and Anticipated Authoritative Guidance sections below.

**penalty_summary (required slot):** The captured Federal Register text states, verbatim: "Under section 203 of the CAA, sales of vehicles are prohibited unless the vehicle is covered by a certificate of conformity, and EPA issues certificates of conformity pursuant to section 206 of the CAA." *Legal Confirmation Required:* No specific civil penalty dollar figure for a Phase 3 GHG violation is stated verbatim in the captured pool text; the enforcement mechanism captured here is the sale prohibition tied to certification, not a stated fine schedule.

### Why This Regulation Is Relevant to the Workspace

*Operational implication:* For a workspace that operates, contracts, or manages a road freight fleet as a primary or secondary transport mode, and whose cargo verticals require dedicated heavy-duty trucking, the Phase 3 rule reshapes the composition, cost, and availability of the HD vehicle fleet from which contracted or owned capacity is drawn. The vehicle manufacturers that supply the workspace's road fleet must comply with these standards; that compliance converts into procurement timelines, vehicle specifications, and per-mile operating costs the workspace encounters as a fleet operator, shipper, or freight forwarder.

*Operational implication:* For a workspace that contracts road haulage rather than owning trucks, the effect is indirect: the rule changes what vehicles carriers can supply from MY 2027 onward and raises upstream manufacturer costs that carriers may seek to pass through in rates.

# 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

### 1. Fleet Procurement Specification Review, WINDOW CLOSING

**Assess** whether any road freight capacity currently contracted or owned includes heavy-duty vehicles that will require replacement or upgrade in the MY 2027 to MY 2032 window.

*Operational implication:* Phase 3 standards begin with MY 2027, meaning vehicles manufactured for sale in the United States from that model year onward must meet the new standards. Fleet replacement cycles of five to ten years mean procurement decisions made in 2024 through 2026 determine whether the workspace's road capacity is standard-compliant from the outset of Phase 3 or requires mid-cycle replacement.

### 2. Carrier Contract Review for Cost Pass-Through, COST ALERT

**Review** existing road carrier contracts for provisions governing fuel surcharges, emissions-compliance cost pass-through, and vehicle specification requirements.

*Operational implication:* Carriers facing higher per-unit compliance costs for compliant vehicles in MY 2027 and beyond will seek to recover costs through rate structures. Contracts that do not anticipate this mechanism may expose the workspace to unplanned cost increases without corresponding client pass-through rights.

### 3. State ACT Program Exposure, MONITORING

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Engage counsel to confirm whether any route operated by the workspace's contracted or owned fleet passes through a state that has adopted the Advanced Clean Trucks (ACT) program under Clean Air Act section 177, which operates alongside this federal rule. This brief addresses the federal Phase 3 rule only.

# 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

*Analytical inference:* The Phase 3 rule imposes its GHG standards on manufacturers of heavy-duty vehicles and engines. Compliance obligations, meeting the per-subcategory standards, demonstrating compliance through the Averaging, Banking, and Trading (ABT) program, and maintaining required documentation, fall on manufacturers as defined under the Clean Air Act and the rule's own definitions.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether any entity in the workspace's supply chain, including the workspace itself if it owns a fleet and imports vehicles, or any carrier it contracts, meets the regulatory definition of "manufacturer" or "importer" under the Clean Air Act for Phase 3 purposes is a legal determination this brief does not make.

### Indirect Position: Freight Forwarder, Shipper, or Fleet Operator

*Analytical inference:* In the standard freight-forwarding transactional structure, the workspace operates as a freight forwarder or shipper, not as a vehicle manufacturer, and does not hold direct Phase 3 compliance obligations in that role. The workspace is downstream of the compliance chain in two ways:

1. As a fleet operator or lessee, the workspace must procure vehicles that manufacturers have built to Phase 3 standards; the workspace does not independently certify vehicles but must ensure its procurement does not specify vehicles that cannot be supplied compliantly after MY 2027. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any specific fleet ownership or leasing arrangement creates a direct regulatory obligation beyond procurement.

2. As a shipper or forwarder contracting road carriers, the workspace holds no direct Phase 3 obligation but faces commercial and cost consequences when carriers' compliance costs change rate structures.

# 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis

### A. Regulatory Lineage

The captured Federal Register text states, verbatim: "76 FR 57106, September 15, 2011" as the citation for the HD GHG Phase 1 rule (2011 on the platform's own timeline), and, verbatim: "81 FR 73478, October 25, 2016" as the citation for the HD GHG Phase 2 rule (2016 on the platform's own timeline, covering MY 2019 to MY 2027). *Analytical inference:* Phase 3 is the third rulemaking in this lineage.

The captured text also states, verbatim: "In 2009, the Administrator issued an Endangerment Finding under CAA section 202(a)", the statutory predicate for EPA's heavy-duty GHG standard-setting authority. *Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether and when that finding is rescinded bears on the durability of the entire GHG standard-setting authority chain; the platform's own timeline records a 2026 EPA action captioned as finalizing repeal of the 2009 endangerment finding, discussed further in the Anticipated Authoritative Guidance section below.

### B. State ACT Program Interaction

The captured text states, verbatim: "the State of California and ten other states have adopted the Advanced Clean Trucks (ACT) program that includes a manufacturer requirement for zero- emission truck sales", and, verbatim: "Vermont adopted ACT beginning in MY 2026". *Analytical inference:* The platform's own timeline separately records a 2026 California CCFR rebate-program milestone and a 2026 Vermont ACT enforcement-pause-expiry milestone; the captured federal rule text corroborates that California and Vermont operate ACT-type programs generally but does not itself state either specific figure or date, which are carried here from the platform's existing timeline record rather than independently re-derived from this document.

*Analytical inference:* The captured text also states, verbatim: "high freight corridors in non-ACT states (including Pennsylvania, Texas, Arizona, and Illinois)", characterizing Pennsylvania as a non-ACT state. The platform's own timeline separately records a 2028 "Pennsylvania ACT enforcement suspension expires" milestone, which presumes an active Pennsylvania ACT program. *Legal Confirmation Required:* This apparent tension (a later Pennsylvania ACT adoption postdating this rule's own analysis, or an alternate explanation) is not resolved by the captured source text and should be confirmed directly against Pennsylvania's Advanced Clean Trucks program status before this milestone is relied upon.

### C. Pending Political and Administrative Developments

*Analytical inference:* The captured EPA summary page states, verbatim: "EPA Announces Action to Implement POTUS’s Termination of Biden-Harris Electric Vehicle Mandate", and separately references, verbatim: "Fact Sheet: Heavy-Duty Vehicles: Powering the Great American Comeback (pdf) (116.41 KB, March 2025)". The platform's own timeline records a 2025 executive-order milestone and a 2025 EPA reconsideration-announcement milestone; the captured source corroborates the underlying political development and dates the associated fact sheet to March 2025, without itself stating a day-level date for either milestone carried on the platform's timeline.

The captured EPA summary page also states, verbatim: "Final Rule: Rescission of the Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and Motor Vehicle Greenhouse Gas Emission Standards Under the Clean Air Act", which corroborates the general direction of the platform's 2026 timeline milestone without itself stating that date.

# 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

*Analytical inference:* Since this rule's 2024 publication (April 22, 2024, 89 FR 29440), several developments bear on its durability and on adjacent state programs the workspace may also encounter:

- 2025: A change in presidential administration accompanied an executive order mandating review of energy-related regulations, per the platform's own timeline; the captured EPA summary page corroborates the underlying political development (see Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis section C above for the verbatim citation).
- 2025: The EPA Administrator is recorded as announcing formal reconsideration of the Phase 3 GHG rule, per the platform's own timeline; the captured EPA summary page's own March 2025 fact sheet reference corroborates the general timeframe.
- 2026: EPA is recorded as finalizing repeal of the 2009 endangerment finding, per the platform's own timeline; the captured EPA summary page's own reference to a rescission final rule corroborates the general direction of this development. *Legal Confirmation Required:* Rescission of the endangerment finding, if finalized, would remove the statutory predicate this rule itself relies on (see Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis section A above); whether and how that repeal affects this Phase 3 rule's own continued validity is a legal question this brief does not resolve.
- 2026: California's CCFR program is recorded as launching an electric truck rebate program, per the platform's own timeline; not independently corroborated at the state-program level by the captured federal rule text (see Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis section B above).
- 2026: Vermont's ACT enforcement pause is recorded as expiring, per the platform's own timeline; the captured federal rule text corroborates only that Vermont operates an ACT program generally, not this specific pause or its expiry date.
- 2028: Pennsylvania's ACT enforcement suspension is recorded as expiring, per the platform's own timeline. *Legal Confirmation Required:* see the tension flagged in Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis section B above between this milestone and the captured text's own characterization of Pennsylvania as a non-ACT state.

*Analytical inference:* None of these developments change the Phase 3 rule's own MY 2027 first-compliance-year status as captured in this brief; a workspace planning fleet procurement should re-check EPA's own Phase 3 rulemaking docket periodically given the reconsideration proceeding referenced above.

# 7. Threshold Questions

### Q1: Does the regulation apply directly to the workspace?

**Decided (with qualification):** The Phase 3 rule's primary compliance obligations fall on HD vehicle and engine manufacturers as defined under the Clean Air Act. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any entity in the workspace's structure meets that definition. For a workspace that is purely a freight forwarder, shipper, or fleet operator purchasing compliant vehicles from third-party manufacturers, the regulation does not impose direct GHG certification or reporting obligations on the workspace under the manufacturer-facing framework.

### Q2: What is the MY 2027 first-compliance threshold for combination tractors?

**Research gap:** Specific numerical CO2 g/ton-mile values for MY 2027 combination tractor subcategories are rendered as embedded graphics (TIFF images) in the captured Federal Register text and are not available as extractable verbatim text spans. A workspace should confirm the numerical thresholds directly from the rule's own regulatory tables.

### Q3: Does the ABT program allow a manufacturer to sell a non-compliant vehicle to the workspace after MY 2027?

*Analytical inference:* Under the ABT framework, a manufacturer may produce individual vehicles exceeding the standard if it holds sufficient banked credits to offset the deficit at the fleet level. This means an individual vehicle ordered by the workspace after MY 2027 could theoretically exceed the standard if the manufacturer's ABT position supports it. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any vehicle-level sale restriction prevents sale of an over-standard vehicle regardless of ABT credit position.

### Q4: Are used HD vehicles in scope?

*Analytical inference:* Phase 3, like its predecessors, establishes standards for new heavy-duty vehicles at the point of manufacture and first sale. A used vehicle already in service is not required to be retrofitted to meet Phase 3 standards under this rule. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any state-level rule imposes a retrofit or retirement obligation on a used HD vehicle in the workspace's fleet.

# 8. Substantive Requirements

### 1. Model-Year CO2 Standard Trajectory (Manufacturer-Facing)

*Analytical inference:* The regulation establishes progressively tightening CO2 emission standards for heavy-duty vehicle and engine subcategories. The captured text states, verbatim: "which finalizes certain revised HD vehicle carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) standards for MY 2027 and certain new HD vehicle CO 2 standards for MYs 2028, 2029, 2030, 2031, and 2032 that will achieve significant GHG reductions for these and later model years. (Note that the MY 2032 standards will remain in place for MY 2033 and thereafter unless and until new standards are promulgated.)"

*Analytical inference:* Specific numerical CO2 g/ton-mile (tractors) and CO2 g/vehicle-mile (vocational vehicles) targets by subcategory and model year are rendered as embedded graphics (TIFF images) in the captured Federal Register text (Tables ES-1 and ES-2) and are not available as extractable verbatim text spans; a workspace should consult the rule's own regulatory tables directly.

### 2. Compliance Basis: Fleet Average, Not Per-Unit

*Analytical inference:* Standards are calculated as fleet averages under the Averaging, Banking, and Trading (ABT) program, not on a unit-by-unit basis. The captured text states, verbatim: "The regulatory provisions for demonstrating compliance with emissions standards have been successfully implemented for decades, including through our Averaging, Banking, and Trading (ABT) program." *Operational implication:* A specific vehicle a workspace orders may perform above or below the fleet-average standard; the standard-setting numbers are fleet averages, not guaranteed per-unit ceilings.

### 3. Family Emission Limit and Credit Banking

The captured text states, verbatim: "For each family or subfamily, the manufacturer must designate a ``Family Emission Limit'', which is an ``emission level . . . to serve in place of the otherwise applicable emission standard'' for each family or subfamily." *Operational implication:* Manufacturers group vehicles into families for compliance purposes; a workspace procuring a specific configuration does not itself see this designation but can request manufacturer compliance documentation as part of due diligence.

### 4. Compliance Demonstration via GEM

The captured text states, verbatim: "Greenhouse gas Emissions Model (GEM) means the GEM simulation tool described in Sec. 1037.520 (incorporated by reference, see Sec. 1037.810)." *Operational implication:* GEM-based compliance determination is a manufacturer-facing technical obligation; a workspace cannot independently verify GEM results but can request manufacturer compliance documentation.

### 5. Useful Life Minimum Values

The captured text states, verbatim: "CAA section 202(d) establishes ``useful life'' minimum values of 10 years or 100,000 miles, whichever occurs first, unless EPA determines that greater values are appropriate."

### 6. General Applicability and Exception

The captured text states, verbatim: "The regulations in this part apply for all new heavy-duty vehicles, except as provided in Sec. 1037.5. This includes battery electric vehicles, fuel cell electric vehicles, and vehicles fueled by conventional and alternative fuels."

### 7. A Scope-Limited Standard Example

The captured text states, verbatim: "The air conditioning leakage standard of Sec. 1037.115 does not apply for model year 2020 and earlier vocational vehicles."

### 8. Small Manufacturer Provisions

The captured text states, verbatim: "qualifying small manufacturers will remain subject to the previously promulgated Phase 2 MY 2027 and later GHG vehicle emission standards, and are not subject to the Phase 3 standards unless they voluntarily decide to opt into the Phase 3 program". *Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether any carrier or vehicle supplier in the workspace's supply chain qualifies as a small manufacturer under the rule's definitions is a legal and factual question requiring carrier-level inquiry.

### 9. Glider Vehicle Treatment

The captured text states, verbatim: "Glider vehicles conforming to the requirements in this paragraph (t)(1) are exempt from the Phase 1 emission standards of this part 1037 prior to January 1, 2021." *Analytical inference:* This provision concerns the predecessor Phase 1 framework's own glider treatment (engines in such vehicles remain independently subject to 40 CFR part 86); a workspace contracting specialized or reconditioned equipment should confirm current glider treatment directly with the manufacturer.

### 10. Certification and Sale Prohibition (Enforcement Mechanism)

The captured text states, verbatim: "Under section 203 of the CAA, sales of vehicles are prohibited unless the vehicle is covered by a certificate of conformity, and EPA issues certificates of conformity pursuant to section 206 of the CAA." *Legal Confirmation Required:* No specific civil penalty dollar figure for a Phase 3 GHG violation is stated verbatim in the captured pool text; the enforcement mechanism captured here is the sale prohibition tied to certification, not a stated fine schedule.

### 11. Statutory Authority

The captured text states, verbatim: "Authority: 42 U.S.C. 7401-7671q."

Obligations surveyed: 14; workspace-adjacent: 14; extracted as FACT: 11.
Shortfall: the per-subcategory numeric CO2 g/ton-mile and g/vehicle-mile emission standard tables (rendered as embedded graphics/TIFF images in the Federal Register text), the specific Clean Air Act civil-penalty dollar amount for an HD GHG violation, and the ZEV/NZEV credit multiplier values are not present as extractable verbatim text in the captured pool and could not be extracted as FACT claims.

# 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

### Manufacturer-Facing Obligations

*Analytical inference:* The Phase 3 rule imposes manufacturer registration, reporting, and record-keeping obligations as part of the compliance demonstration framework, including submitting GEM compliance reports to EPA, maintaining records of ABT credit generation, banking, and trading transactions, and reporting certificate of conformity information. Specific record-keeping formats and submission schedules are not available as verbatim spans in the captured pool text.

### Workspace-Level Reporting Implications

*Operational implication:* For a workspace that reports Scope 3 emissions to clients, investors, or under a disclosure regime, the Phase 3 rule does not create a direct registration or reporting obligation for the workspace. It does create a market condition in which vehicle GHG performance data generated by manufacturers through GEM becomes available and is increasingly expected as the basis for Scope 3 freight emission calculations. A workspace relying on spend-based or generic distance-based Scope 3 methods may face pressure to migrate to vehicle-activity-based accounting consistent with the performance categories Phase 3 establishes.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether the workspace has a direct registration or reporting obligation under Phase 3, as distinct from manufacturers, is a legal question; based on the rule's structure, direct obligations fall on manufacturers.

# 11. Operational System Requirements

### 1. Fleet Procurement Specification Update

**Scope:** Road fleet procurement specifications, carrier contract requirements, and vehicle replacement planning.

**Deadline:** Effective from MY 2027 vehicle production; procurement decisions affecting MY 2027 deliveries should be made no later than 2025 to 2026, depending on OEM lead times.

*Operational implication:* A workspace operating or contracting fleets on multi-year replacement cycles without a Phase 3 vehicle specification requirement embedded in procurement criteria faces a gap: a vehicle ordered without Phase 3-aligned specifications from MY 2027 onward may not be available from a manufacturer operating under ABT deficits.

### 2. Carrier Emissions Data Collection Infrastructure

*Analytical inference:* Client sustainability reporting requirements (CSRD for EU-operating clients, the SEC climate disclosure rule for U.S.-listed counterparties) will increasingly demand vehicle-level or carrier-level GHG performance data rather than spend-based estimates.

*Operational implication:* A workspace currently calculating Scope 3 freight emissions using the spend-based method without carrier-provided vehicle activity data cannot distinguish an MY 2021-era Phase 2 vehicle from an MY 2027 Phase 3-compliant vehicle in its emissions accounting.

### 3. Contract Clause Review: Carrier GHG Compliance Attestation

*Analytical inference:* Standard freight carrier contracts do not typically include vehicle-model-year or emission-standard attestation clauses. Adding such language ahead of MY 2027 gives the workspace a contractual basis to help ensure Phase 3-compliant capacity.

# 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

### 1. Small Manufacturer Provisions

See Substantive Requirements section 8 above for the captured verbatim small-manufacturer opt-in language. *Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether any carrier or vehicle supplier in the workspace's supply chain qualifies as a small manufacturer is a legal and factual question requiring carrier-level inquiry.

### 2. Glider Vehicles

See Substantive Requirements section 8 above for the captured verbatim Phase 1 glider exemption language. *Analytical inference:* A workspace contracting reconditioned or glider-kit equipment should confirm current treatment directly with the manufacturer, since the captured span concerns the predecessor Phase 1 framework specifically.

### 3. Vehicles Not Sold for U.S. Operation

*Analytical inference:* Phase 3 standards apply to vehicles sold into the U.S. market; a vehicle manufactured for export and not sold in the United States is not subject to this rule under EPA's Clean Air Act jurisdiction. *Legal Confirmation Required:* For a workspace with cross-border operations involving Canadian or Mexican trucking, what vehicle emission standards apply in those jurisdictions, and whether they align with, exceed, or fall below Phase 3 levels.

### 4. Air Conditioning Leakage Scope Exception

See Substantive Requirements section 8 above for the captured verbatim scope-limit language on the air conditioning leakage standard.

# 13. Adjacent Industry Research and Alternatives

*Note: This section summarizes context relevant to the Phase 3 rule's operational environment. Claims are labeled as to source tier where applicable.*

### 1. Zero-Emission Truck Technology Readiness

*Industry interpretation:* Independent industry analyses (for example, from the International Council on Clean Transportation and the Rocky Mountain Institute) examine the cost and performance trajectory of battery-electric and hydrogen fuel cell Class 8 trucks, the primary technology pathways relevant to Phase 3 compliance. These are not part of the captured source pool for this item and are not cited as FACT here; a workspace should treat this as background context pending independent verification.

### 2. Charging and Fueling Infrastructure

*Analytical inference:* Heavy-duty truck charging and hydrogen fueling infrastructure remain at an early deployment stage relative to the MY 2027 to MY 2032 compliance window. *Operational implication:* For a workspace operating long-haul routes that currently lack HD charging infrastructure at key waypoints, the pace of infrastructure deployment is a binding constraint on how quickly zero-emission tractors can be operationally deployed, independent of manufacturer compliance schedules.

# 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 2011: Phase 1 GHG rule finalized (76 FR 57106, September 15, 2011)
- 2016: Phase 2 GHG rule finalized (81 FR 73478, October 25, 2016) (MY 2019 to 2027)
- 2024: Phase 3 GHG final rule published, 89 FR 29440 (April 22, 2024)
- 2024: Phase 3 effective date (June 21, 2024)
- 2025: Trump administration takes office; executive order mandating review of energy related regulations
- 2025: EPA Administrator announces formal reconsideration of Phase 3 GHG
- 2026: EPA finalizes repeal of the 2009 endangerment finding
- 2026: California CCFR electric truck rebate program launches
- 2026: Vermont ACT enforcement pause expires
- 2028: Pennsylvania ACT enforcement suspension expires

*Source note:* The captured Federal Register text states, verbatim: "This final rule is effective on June 21, 2024." and, verbatim: "Federal Register, Volume 89 Issue 78 (Monday, April 22, 2024)". The Phase 1, Phase 2, EPA reconsideration, endangerment-finding-repeal, and state ACT/CCFR program milestones above are carried from the platform's existing timeline record for this item, at year precision only (the captured pool does not independently state day-level dates for those milestones); see Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis and Anticipated Authoritative Guidance sections above for the verbatim source text that corroborates each, including the honest scope limits on that corroboration.

entries.body:
# 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document synthesizes publicly available information from Oregon DEQ's authoritative web presence to provide freight-forwarding workspaces with a structured intelligence brief on Oregon's principal environmental compliance frameworks. The DEQ operates as Oregon's central environmental regulatory body, administering air quality, water quality, land quality, climate protection, and clean fuels programs. Each of these frameworks carries compliance obligations that may intersect with freight operations involving diesel fuel importation, vehicle emissions, greenhouse gas reporting, and waste management.

**Convention notes:**
- "The workspace" refers to a global freight forwarding operation with air-primary, road-secondary, and ocean-tertiary transport modes, operating across Americas, European, and Asian trade lanes.
- All FACT claims are span-grounded to verbatim text within the SOURCE corpus. ANALYSIS is labeled with the required prefix tokens.
- Items requiring legal review are labeled *Legal Confirmation Required:*
- Date of generation: most recent authoring pass

# 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

Oregon DEQ is not itself a single regulation; it is the administering authority for a portfolio of environmental compliance programs established under Oregon state law. The two programs most relevant to freight forwarding operations are the Climate Protection Program (CPP) and the Clean Fuels Program (CFP).

**1. Oregon Climate Protection Program (CPP)**

FACT: "The Climate Protection Program is critical to meeting Oregon's greenhouse gas reduction goals. The program establishes a declining cap, or limit, on greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels used throughout Oregon, including diesel, gasoline, and natural gas." *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

FACT: "The program is designed to reduce these emissions 50% by 2035 and 90% by 2050." *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

FACT: "The first compliance period starts Jan. 1, 2025, and covers emissions through the end of 2027." *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

**Effective date slot:** FACT: The CPP first compliance period starts Jan. 1, 2025, as stated in the source above.

**2. Oregon Clean Fuels Program (CFP)**

FACT: "Oregon’s Clean Fuels Program (CFP) was initiated in 2009 when the legislature passed HB 2186, empowering the Oregon Environmental Quality Commission (EQC) to “adopt by rule low carbon fuel standards for gasoline, diesel and fuels used as substitutes for gasoline or diesel.”" *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

FACT: "Implemented in 2016, five years after California’s LCFS, the CFP has evolved over time." *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

FACT: The CPP is governed by "OAR Chapter 340, Division 273". *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

**Jurisdictional scope slot:** FACT: The DEQ's programs apply to operations in Oregon, covering fossil fuels used throughout Oregon, per the CPP passage quoted above.

**Why it applies to the workspace:** Freight forwarding operations with road transport in Oregon, particularly those importing diesel, operating vehicle fleets on Oregon roads, or managing natural gas infrastructure, fall within the scope of programs administered by Oregon DEQ. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, depending on its specific transactional role (importer of record vs. freight agent vs. fuel dispenser), constitutes a "regulated party" or "registered party" as defined under OAR Chapter 340, Division 253 (CFP) or OAR Chapter 340, Division 273 (CPP) requires counsel review against those specific definitional articles.

# 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

## MONITORING: CPP First Compliance Period In Progress

**Assess** whether any Oregon-based fuel supply, fleet fueling, or logistics hub operations place the workspace in a "regulated company" role under the CPP's first compliance period (Jan. 1, 2025 to Dec. 31, 2027).

FACT: "Each year, DEQ distributes a set number of free compliance instruments to regulated companies. The total number of compliance instruments distributed by DEQ each year is equal to that year's emissions cap." *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

FACT: "The program gives regulated companies the option to bank compliance instruments if they emit less than the number of compliance instruments they receive, trade compliance instruments with other regulated companies, or earn additional credits by contributing funds to DEQ-approved entities through the Community Climate Investments program." *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

*Operational implication:* For workspaces operating Oregon road fleets fueled by diesel, *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace's diesel consumption volume triggers "regulated company" classification under the CPP and what compliance instrument obligations attach.

## WINDOW CLOSING: Clean Fuels Program Annual Report Deadline

**Verify** compliance status for any Oregon fuel import or dispensing activity against the CFP annual reporting cycle.

FACT: "Regulated parties must comply with the Clean Fuel Standards by balancing their credits and deficits for each calendar year by the annual report deadline." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

FACT: The CFP credit market's recent price movement is tied to "the April 30 deadline for filing final 2025 compliance reports where each entity’s cumulative deficits must be covered by credits in their account." *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

*Operational implication:* The April 30 annual compliance deadline creates a defined credit-procurement window. Workspaces that may be classified as regulated parties under the CFP and who have not pre-positioned credits risk a credit clearance market exposure at elevated prices.

## ACTION REQUIRED: Vehicle Inspection Compliance (Oregon Road Operations)

**Map** all Oregon-operated vehicles to DEQ vehicle inspection program requirements.

FACT: The DEQ website lists "Portland area: Clackamas Station Gresham Station NE Portland Station Sherwood Station Sunset / Hillsboro Station Scappoose Station Medford Station" as Clean Air Stations. *Source: Oregon DEQ Welcome Page, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://oregon.gov/deq/Pages/index.aspx

*Operational implication:* Oregon road operations using diesel-powered fleet vehicles are subject to vehicle inspection requirements administered by DEQ. Failure to maintain inspection compliance exposes the workspace to enforcement under OAR Chapter 340, Division 12.

## MONITORING: 2026-2027 CFP Rulemaking

**Engage** with Oregon DEQ's 2026-2027 CFP rulemaking process to track proposed CI reduction schedule changes that would increase compliance costs for diesel-consuming road operations. See section 6 below for the full forward-looking detail.

# 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

Oregon DEQ programs establish obligations along a supply and transport chain. The relevant chain positions for freight operations are:

**Clean Fuels Program chain:**

FACT: "Importers of gasoline, diesel, ethanol, biodiesel, and renewable diesel and in-state producers of any transportation fuel are required to participate." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

FACT: "In addition, providers of natural gas (owner of the dispenser), propane (owner of the dispenser), electricity (owner of the charger or the electric utility), and hydrogen (owner of the fuel) can choose to participate if they wish to generate credits." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, in its role as a freight forwarder that may arrange diesel importation into Oregon on behalf of clients, constitutes an "importer" as that term is defined in OAR 340-253 (CFP) or OAR 340-273 (CPP), or whether the importing obligation attaches to the entity of record on the import documentation. This is a legal determination, not an operational one.

**Climate Protection Program chain:**

*Analytical inference:* The CPP's cap-and-trade structure means compliance costs incurred by upstream fuel suppliers (diesel distributors, natural gas utilities) will be passed through to commercial consumers of those fuels, including freight operators, through higher fuel prices, whether or not the workspace is itself a "regulated company" under the CPP.

**Enforcement chain:**

FACT: "DEQ achieves compliance through a number of tools including, technical assistance, inspections, complaint investigations, and orders to pay fines and perform corrective actions." *Source: Oregon DEQ Compliance and Enforcement, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/DEQ/Regulations/Pages/Compliance-and-Enforcement.aspx

FACT: "The Oregon Department of Environmental Quality enforces the law and focuses its compliance resources on the most serious environmental violations to ensure that people in Oregon may enjoy a healthy environment." *Source: Oregon DEQ Compliance and Enforcement, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/DEQ/Regulations/Pages/Compliance-and-Enforcement.aspx

# 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis

## Climate Protection Program: Program Design

FACT: The CPP is governed by "OAR Chapter 340, Division 273". *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

FACT: The program "Supports reductions in other types of air pollution.   Enhances public welfare, particularly for environmental justice communities, including communities of color, tribal, low-income, and rural communities. Provides regulated companies with compliance flexibility options to manage their costs.  Supports a strong statewide economy. Prioritizes equity by promoting benefits and reducing burdens for environmental justice communities most impacted by pollution and with less access to cleaner energy alternatives." *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

*Operational implication:* The equity focus of the CPP, explicitly including rural communities, suggests the program's Community Climate Investment pathway may represent a compliance mechanism available even to operators with distributed rural Oregon operations, but *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace would qualify to generate or retire Community Climate Investment credits.

## Clean Fuels Program: Structure and Standards

FACT: "DEQ has identified the carbon intensity, or level of carbon emissions, for each type of available fuel, with diesel and gasoline having the highest carbon intensity. Each year, DEQ sets the level of carbon intensity of transportation fuels used in Oregon. DEQ requires fuel providers to show that the volume and type of fuel they supply for use in Oregon meets the carbon intensity level, or standard, for that year. DEQ gradually lowers the amount of carbon intensity in fuel allowed each year to meet the annual reduction goal." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

FACT: "Businesses that create fuels that are cleaner than the annual limit generate credits, while higher carbon intensity fuels create deficits. Credits and deficits are measured in metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

FACT: "Examples of such projects are installations of electric charging stations and dairy manure digesters that inject methane into natural gas pipelines." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

**Full per-year trajectory (CFP carbon intensity reduction schedule):**

FACT: "The baseline year for the program is 2015 and the standard for that year represents 10 percent ethanol blended with gasoline and 5 percent biodiesel blended with diesel." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

FACT: "The current rule requires a 10 percent reduction in average carbon intensity from 2015 levels by 2025, followed by a 20 percent reduction by 2030 and 37 percent by 2035." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

*Analytical inference:* FACT (extended trajectory): "On September 23, 2022, the EQC unanimously approved a significant expansion of the CFP , setting more stringent benchmark standards: a 20% CI reduction by 2030 and a 37% reduction by 2035. These extended and more aggressive standards, displayed in Figure 1 below, took effect January 1, 2023." *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

*Analytical inference:* FACT (technical update): "On January 9, 2025, the EQC approved the CFP 2024 rulemaking which made primarily administrative adjustments to the program’s supporting rules, adopted the OR-GREET 4.0 model to calculate fuels’ lifecycle CIs, added a reserve account framework for credits from carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) fuel pathways, introduced additional tracking requirements for high-risk feedstocks, and required electricity reporting and fuel pathway applications to go through third-party verification." *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

FACT: "With the new version of the GREET model, the default CI for clear gasoline declined from 100.14 to 98.12 grams of carbon dioxide equivalents per megajoule (gCO 2 e/MJ or g/MJ) and the default CI for petroleum diesel rose from 100.74 to 104.92 g/MJ." *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

*Operational implication:* The increase in petroleum diesel's default CI under OR-GREET 4.0 (from 100.74 to 104.92 g/MJ) means that diesel-heavy freight operations in Oregon generate larger per-unit deficits under the CFP than they did prior to January 9, 2025, increasing the credit volume required for compliance.

FACT: "Figure 1. Oregon CFP Carbon Intensity Reduction Schedule Source: Oregon Department of Environmental Quality, OAR 340-253-8010" *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

## Compliance and Enforcement Framework

FACT: "Office of Compliance and Enforcement issues civil penalties and Department Orders on behalf of DEQ’s director, who has been delegated to do so by the Environmental Quality Commission." *Source: Oregon DEQ Compliance and Enforcement, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/DEQ/Regulations/Pages/Compliance-and-Enforcement.aspx

FACT: "The vast majority of penalties are not deposited directly to DEQ and must be deposited to Oregon State General Fund." *Source: Oregon DEQ Compliance and Enforcement, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/DEQ/Regulations/Pages/Compliance-and-Enforcement.aspx

FACT: "An appeal may be resolved through negotiation or a contested case hearing." *Source: Oregon DEQ Compliance and Enforcement, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/DEQ/Regulations/Pages/Compliance-and-Enforcement.aspx

## Environmental Justice Framework

FACT: "Oregon’s environmental justice law, established in 2008, requires state natural resource agencies – including DEQ and 13 other agencies – to follow prescribed steps to provide greater public participation and ensure involvement of people who may be affected by agency actions." *Source: Oregon DEQ Environmental Justice, State Laws and Policy, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/about-us/pages/environmental-justice-laws.aspx

FACT: "Senate Bill 420, which created the law, also created an Environmental Justice Task Force." *Source: Oregon DEQ Environmental Justice, State Laws and Policy, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/about-us/pages/environmental-justice-laws.aspx

FACT: "The Task Force, consisting of 12 members appointed by the governor, is charged with: Advising the Governor on environmental justice issues." *Source: Oregon DEQ Environmental Justice, State Laws and Policy, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/about-us/pages/environmental-justice-laws.aspx

*Operational implication:* Freight operations sited in or proximate to communities defined as environmental justice communities under Oregon law may attract heightened DEQ scrutiny and community participation obligations attached to permit applications or enforcement proceedings.

## Statewide Transportation Strategy

FACT: "Executive Order 20-04 directs DEQ, the Oregon Department of Transportation, the Department of Land Conservation and Development, the Department of Energy to collaborate and identify specific actions to help the state get back on track with the Oregon Statewide Transportation Strategy: A 2050 Vision For Greenhouse Gas Reduction vision and the Governor’s new reduction goals in Executive Order 20-04 to reduce greenhouse gas pollution to at least 45 percent below 1990 emissions levels by 2035 and to at least 80 percent below 1990 emissions by 2050." *Source: Oregon DEQ Implementation of the Statewide Transportation Strategy, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/Pages/Transportation-Strategy.aspx

*Operational implication:* For workspaces with medium- and heavy-duty truck operations in Oregon, the multi-agency Statewide Transportation Strategy implementation may generate additional regulatory requirements through parallel rulemaking at ODOT, DLCD, and the Department of Energy, not only through DEQ. Monitoring these adjacent agencies' rulemaking pipelines is operationally necessary.

# 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

## MONITORING: CFP 2026-2027 Rulemaking (CI Reduction Extension to 2040)

**Event type:** Formal rulemaking, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking
**Issuing body:** Oregon DEQ / Oregon Environmental Quality Commission

FACT: "on November 20, 2025, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek issued Executive Order 25-29, directing DEQ and the EQC to strengthen the CFP by establishing a new CI reduction requirement of at least 50% by 2040 and to better align Oregon’s program with neighboring jurisdictions." *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

FACT: "In response, DEQ launched a 2026-2027 rulemaking, with a Rulemaking Advisory Committee convened in early 2026, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking anticipated in late 2026, and EQC consideration expected in late 2026 or early 2027." *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

*Analytical inference:* FACT: "The rulemaking is expected to extend CFP targets to at least 2040, evaluate whether to adjust existing standards before 2035, address transportation electrification, and fix issues in the offsite renewable electricity provisions." *Source: Stillwater CFP 101, Stillwater Associates, May 29, 2026. https://stillwaterpublications.com/stillwater-cfp-101/

*Operational implication:* If the EQC adopts the at-least-50-percent CI reduction by 2040, diesel-intensive road operations in Oregon face a steeper compliance cost trajectory post-2035 than currently in force. The rulemaking advisory period (early 2026 and ongoing) represents a window to submit comments affecting how the standard is applied to transport and logistics entities.

**Re-check window:** Late 2026 (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking anticipated); EQC vote expected late 2026 or early 2027.

## Anticipated Standing Obligations Reaffirmed by the Source as of 2026

The captured source's own registered-parties requirements (Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, active as of 2026) restate the following recurring, standing duties. They are carried here individually, per the forward-intelligence discipline, rather than left as database rows the brief's own reader-facing prose never mentions:

1. **Registration duty (recurring, standing as of 2026).** FACT: Registered parties must "Register with DEQ before producing fuel in Oregon, importing fuel into Oregon, dispensing certain fuels into motor vehicles, or generating or transacting credits for fuels supplied in Oregon." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

2. **Record-keeping duty (recurring, standing as of 2026).** FACT: Registered parties must "Keep records for each transaction of transportation fuel imported, sold or supplied for use in Oregon." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

3. **Quarterly and annual reporting duty (recurring, standing as of 2026).** FACT: Registered parties must "Submit quarterly and annual reports using the Oregon Fuels Reporting System." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

4. **CI reduction step-down (dated milestones, 2030 and 2035).** FACT: "The current rule requires a 10 percent reduction in average carbon intensity from 2015 levels by 2025, followed by a 20 percent reduction by 2030 and 37 percent by 2035." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

5. **Penalty adjustment authority (standing as of 2026).** FACT: "Base penalties may be increased or decreased depending on specific factors according to Division 12." *Source: Oregon DEQ Compliance and Enforcement, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/DEQ/Regulations/Pages/Compliance-and-Enforcement.aspx

6. **2015 baseline reference (background, standing as of 2026).** FACT: "The baseline year for the program is 2015 and the standard for that year represents 10 percent ethanol blended with gasoline and 5 percent biodiesel blended with diesel." *Source: Oregon DEQ Clean Fuels Program Overview, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cfp/pages/cfp-overview.aspx

*Operational implication:* None of these six items is a one-time deadline; each is a standing, recurring obligation or reference point the source restates as currently in force. A workspace that is a CFP registered party must maintain registration, per-transaction records, and quarterly/annual reporting continuously, not only at a single forward date; the 2030 and 2035 CI step-downs are the only two of the six with genuine future dates attached.

## MONITORING: CPP 2024 Rulemaking / Emissions-Intensive Trade-Exposed Rulemaking

FACT: The DEQ website references "Emissions-Intensive Trade-Exposed Rulemaking Climate Protection Program 2024 Rulemaking" as distinct sub-programs under the CPP. *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

*Analytical inference:* The specific rulemaking schedule and outcomes for the Emissions-Intensive Trade-Exposed Rulemaking are not fully detailed in the source corpus. Research gap: the corpus does not provide the adopted text or outcome dates for the 2024 CPP rulemaking or the EITE rulemaking. Workspaces with Oregon operations should retrieve OAR Chapter 340, Division 273 directly and consult DEQ's rulemaking archive.

# 7. Threshold Questions

## Question 1: Does the workspace qualify as a "regulated company" under the CPP?

**Status:** *Legal Confirmation Required:* The CPP applies to "regulated companies" handling fossil fuels (diesel, gasoline, natural gas) in Oregon. Whether the workspace, as a freight forwarder, logistics operator, or fleet vehicle operator, meets the CPP's defined threshold for "regulated company" turns on the specific definitional terms in OAR Chapter 340, Division 273, which the source corpus does not reproduce verbatim. Counsel review against OAR 340-273 definitions is required before any conclusion on obligation attachment.

## Question 2: Is the workspace a "mandatory regulated party" or "voluntary registered party" under the CFP?

## CPP Requirements (OAR Chapter 340, Division 273)

**Compliance period:**

FACT: "The first compliance period starts Jan. 1, 2025, and covers emissions through the end of 2027." *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

FACT: "For every ton of greenhouse gas emissions a company is responsible for, it must submit a compliance instrument or a Community Climate Investment credit to DEQ." *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx

**Compliance flexibility mechanisms:**

FACT: "The program gives regulated companies the option to bank compliance instruments if they emit less than the number of compliance instruments they receive, trade compliance instruments with other regulated companies, or earn additional credits by contributing funds to DEQ-approved entities through the Community Climate Investments program." *Source: Oregon DEQ Climate Protection Program, Oregon DEQ, active as of 2026. https://www.oregon.gov/deq/ghgp/cpp/pages/default.aspx
